newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Maskhadov becomes Chechen president, vows peace.
newsitem.headline: Maskhadov becomes Chechen president, vows peace.

text.p: Chechnya's first post-war president Aslan Maskhadov took office on Wednesday, pledging to realise the dream of independence for which his ancestors and contemporaries fought Russia.

Maskhadov, a former Soviet artillery colonel who led separatist rebels against Russian troops sent to crush them in December 1994, also promised to strengthen the Moslem religion and fight a crime wave in the shattered region.

"Now it's the duty of each and every one of us to realise the expectations of our ancestors, our heroes fallen in the holy war, of the right to live freely and independently," Maskhadov told rebels and Russian representatives in the Chechen capital.
"For hundreds of years our nation was not allowed to live freely, to be master of its country."

The soft-spoken Maskhadov, who spent the 21-month conflict with Russia in military fatigues, wore a dark suit and a traditional astrakhan fur hat for the ceremony, held in a suburb of Grozny whose centre was flattened in the war.

Behind him on the stage of the suburban assembly hall stood leaders of the rebel force which humiliated the Russian military in fighting which killed tens of thousands of people and left many more homeless.
Alexander Lebed, former security adviser to President Boris Yeltsin, sat in the audience as did Ivan Rybkin, current secretary of Russia's Security Council.

Lebed signed a peace deal with Maskhadov in August, agreeing to pull out troops and bringing fighting to an end. The Chechens, conquered by Tsarist forces over a century ago and sent en masse into internal exile in Central Asia by dictator Josef Stalin during World War Two, now seek full independence.

But Moscow, fearing separatism elsewhere in its vast territories, insists the region is a part of the Russian Federation and will not discuss sovereignty for five years. Foreign governments, unwilling to anger the Kremlin, would also balk at diplomatic recognition.

Outside on the street, after the white-haired Maskhadov, a former Soviet colonel, had sworn an oath in front of commanders of the rebel force, the men let loose with their weapons in a triumphant show of force.
Mothers in the crowd covered their childrens' ears but otherwise did not even flinch at the sound of hundreds of automatic rifles being fired into the air.
But the rebels were generally in peaceful mood.
"We don't intend to fight any more," said Ali Amagayev, lounging around after the ceremony with a group of friends.
Asked what they would do now that the war was over he said they all had different plans. "Some will go to their collective farms, some into commerce, others will stay in the military," he said.
Shamil Basayev, Russia's enemy number one who led a hostage raid inside Russia in 1995 and then stood against Maskhadov in the January poll, was also in an upbeat mood.

"I am very glad that we could carry out this inauguration together so that, just as we fought this war with honour, so with honour we can move to live peacefully on the path to freedom," he said after the ceremony.
Maskhadov promised to bring the myriad armed groups in the region into line and to protect Chechnya's Russian population.

"First of all it's necessary to strengthen the Moslem religion, to free the nation from the violence and mockery of criminal elements. To that I will direct all my efforts. A state cannot consider itself free whose citizens are in constant fear of their lives," he said.
